claims.evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The main finding of a positive correlation between factorization and neural predictivity was robust to the particular choice of PCA threshold used to quantify factorization.
claims.source: Furthermore, the main finding of a positive correlation between factorization and neural predictivity was robust to the particular choice of PCA threshold we used to quantify factorization (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Factorization scores significantly boosted cross-validated predictive power of neural/behavioral fit performance compared to simply using object classification alone.
claims.source: However, we found that factorization scores significantly boosted cross-validated predictive power of neural/behavioral fit performance compared to simply using object classification alone, and factorization boosted predictive power as much if not slightly more when using RDMs instead of linear regression fits to quantify the match to the brain/behavior (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Considering factorization in addition to object classification performance improves upon our prior understanding of the properties of more brainlike models.
claims.source: Thus, considering factorization in addition to object classification performance improves upon our prior understanding of the properties of more brainlike models (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the combined analysis shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Factorization is related to the existing concept of manifold disentanglement.
claims.source: We note that our definition of factorization is closely related to the existing concept of manifold disentanglement (DiCarlo and Cox, 2007; Chung et al., 2018) and can be seen as a generalization of disentanglement to high-dimensional visual scene parameters like object pose.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on manifold disentanglement (DiCarlo and Cox, 2007; Chung et al., 2018).

claims.claim: Factorization can be seen as a generalization of disentanglement to high-dimensional visual scene parameters like object pose.
claims.source: We note that our definition of factorization is closely related to the existing concept of manifold disentanglement (DiCarlo and Cox, 2007; Chung et al., 2018) and can be seen as a generalization of disentanglement to high-dimensional visual scene parameters like object pose.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' conceptual framework relating factorization to disentanglement.

claims.claim: The extent to which variables were represented in a factorized way influenced the ability of a linear discriminator to successfully decode both variables in a generalizable fashion from a few training samples.
claims.source: In a simulation, we found that the extent to which the variables of interest were represented in a factorized way (i.e., along orthogonal axes, rather than correlated axes) influenced the ability of a linear discriminator to successfully decode both variables in a generalizable fashion from a few training samples (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: A linear basis rotation that decreased factorization while leaving all other activity statistics intact had the effect of strongly reducing object identity decoding performance in both V4 and IT.
claims.source: The applied linear basis rotation leaves all other activity statistics completely intact (such as mean neural firing rates, covariance structure of the population, and its invariance to non-class variables) yet has the effect of strongly reducing object identity decoding performance in both V4 and IT (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the lesion experiment data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Factorization of frame-by-frame variance from other sources of variance across natural movies was correlated with improved neural predictivity in both macaque and human data.
claims.source: Similar to the result found for factorization measured using augmentations of synthetic images, factorization of frame-by-frame variance (local in time, presumably dominated by either observer or camera motion; see 'Methods') from other sources of variance across natural movies (non-local in time) was correlated with improved neural predictivity in both macaque and human data while invariance to local frame-by-frame differences was not (Figure 5B; black versus gray bars).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of natural movie data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Invariance to local frame-by-frame differences in natural movies was not correlated with improved neural predictivity.
claims.source: Similar to the result found for factorization measured using augmentations of synthetic images, factorization of frame-by-frame variance (local in time, presumably dominated by either observer or camera motion; see 'Methods') from other sources of variance across natural movies (non-local in time) was correlated with improved neural predictivity in both macaque and human data while invariance to local frame-by-frame differences was not (Figure 5B; black versus gray bars).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of natural movie data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The relationship between factorization and matches to neural data was not entirely mediated by classification or dimensionality.
claims.source: Critically, our results cannot be accounted for by classification performance or dimensionality alone (Figure 6, gray and pink bars); that is, the relationship between factorization and matches to neural data was not entirely mediated by classification or dimensionality.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis controlling for classification and dimensionality shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: High-dimensional representations could be regarded as a means to facilitate factorization.
claims.source: Indeed, high-dimensional representations could be regarded as a means to facilitate factorization, and likewise factorized representations can better support classification (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference about the relationship between dimensionality and factorization, supported by simulation data in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Factorized representations can better support classification.
claims.source: Indeed, high-dimensional representations could be regarded as a means to facilitate factorization, and likewise factorized representations can better support classification (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference about the relationship between factorization and classification, supported by simulation data in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Machine learning models designed to infer disentangled representations of visual data displayed single-unit responses that resembled those of individual neurons in macaque IT.
claims.source: One prior study notably found that machine learning models designed to infer disentangled representations of visual data displayed single-unit responses that resembled those of individual neurons in macaque IT (Higgins et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Higgins et al., 2021).

claims.claim: A fully factorized representation should be highly abstract according to the definition of abstraction in representational geometry.
claims.source: A fully factorized representation should be highly abstract according to this definition, though factorization emphasizes the geometric properties of the population representation while these studies emphasize the consequences for decoding performance in training downstream linear read-outs.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference about the relationship between factorization and abstraction as defined in prior work.

claims.claim: Orthogonal encoding of class and non-class information is one of several factors that determines few-shot classification performance.
claims.source: Relatedly, another recent study found that orthogonal encoding of class and non-class information is one of several factors that determines few-shot classification performance (Sorscher et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Sorscher et al., 2022).

claims.claim: Local straightening of natural movies was found to be important for early visual cortex neural responses but not necessarily for high-level visual cortex.
claims.source: Local straightening of natural movies was found to be important for early visual cortex neural responses but not necessarily for high-level visual cortex (Toosi and Issa, 2022), where the present work suggests factorization may play a role.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Toosi and Issa, 2022).

claims.claim: Factorization may play a role in high-level visual cortex.
claims.source: Local straightening of natural movies was found to be important for early visual cortex neural responses but not necessarily for high-level visual cortex (Toosi and Issa, 2022), where the present work suggests factorization may play a role.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the findings of the present work.

claims.claim: Factorization increases with higher dimensionality as this decreases overlap.
claims.source: Intuitively, factorization increases with higher dimensionality as this decreases overlap, all other things being equal (in the limit, the angle between points will approach 90o or a fully orthogonal code in high dimensions), and for a given finite, fixed dimension, factorization is mainly driven by the angle between this dimension and the other variable subspaces which measures the degree of contamination (Figure 1C; square vs. parallelogram).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on mathematical reasoning about high-dimensional spaces.

claims.claim: In the limit of high dimensions, the angle between points will approach 90 degrees or a fully orthogonal code.
claims.source: Intuitively, factorization increases with higher dimensionality as this decreases overlap, all other things being equal (in the limit, the angle between points will approach 90o or a fully orthogonal code in high dimensions), and for a given finite, fixed dimension, factorization is mainly driven by the angle between this dimension and the other variable subspaces which measures the degree of contamination (Figure 1C; square vs. parallelogram).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on mathematical reasoning about high-dimensional spaces.

claims.claim: For a given finite, fixed dimension, factorization is mainly driven by the angle between this dimension and the other variable subspaces which measures the degree of contamination.
claims.source: Intuitively, factorization increases with higher dimensionality as this decreases overlap, all other things being equal (in the limit, the angle between points will approach 90o or a fully orthogonal code in high dimensions), and for a given finite, fixed dimension, factorization is mainly driven by the angle between this dimension and the other variable subspaces which measures the degree of contamination (Figure 1C; square vs. parallelogram).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on mathematical reasoning about the geometry of factorization.

claims.claim: Invariance to non-identity information was more pronounced when measured in the subspace of population activity capturing the bulk (90%) of identity-driven variance as a consequence of increased factorization of identity from non-identity information.
claims.source: Invariance to non-identity information was even more pronounced when measured in the subspace of population activity capturing the bulk (90%) of identity-driven variance as a consequence of increased factorization of identity from non-identity information (Figure 2A, right, dashed lines).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The normalized factorization scores remained significantly above zero for both V4 and IT brain areas after subtracting shuffle control.
claims.source: Shuffling the image identities of each population vector accounts for increases in factorization driven purely by changes in the covariance statistics of population responses between V4 and IT. However, the normalized factorization scores remained significantly above zero for both brain areas.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The results were preserved when re-running the analyses using only the subset of models with the identical ResNet-50 architecture.
claims.source: Our results were preserved when we re-ran the analyses using only the subset of models with the identical ResNet-50 architecture (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) or when we evaluated model predictivity using representational dissimilarity matrices of the population (RDMs) instead of linear regression (encoding) fits of individual neurons or voxels (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by control analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The results were preserved when evaluating model predictivity using representational dissimilarity matrices of the population (RDMs) instead of linear regression (encoding) fits of individual neurons or voxels.
claims.source: Our results were preserved when we re-ran the analyses using only the subset of models with the identical ResNet-50 architecture (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) or when we evaluated model predictivity using representational dissimilarity matrices of the population (RDMs) instead of linear regression (encoding) fits of individual neurons or voxels (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by control analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Similar results were found using a covariance-based method for computing factorization that does not have any free parameters.
claims.source: We found similar results using a covariance-based method for computing factorization that does not have any free parameters (Figure 5C, faded filled circles; see Equations 4 in 'Methods').
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of two methods shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Factorization of non-class information is an important strategy used, alongside invariance, by the high-level visual cortex.
claims.source: Here, we presented evidence that factorization of non-class information is an important strategy used, alongside invariance, by the high-level visual cortex (Figure 2) and by DNNs that are predictive of primate neural and behavioral data (Figures 4 and 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from neural recordings and DNN model analyses.

claims.claim: Factorization of non-class information is an important strategy used by DNNs that are predictive of primate neural and behavioral data.
claims.source: Here, we presented evidence that factorization of non-class information is an important strategy used, alongside invariance, by the high-level visual cortex (Figure 2) and by DNNs that are predictive of primate neural and behavioral data (Figures 4 and 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by DNN model analyses shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claims.claim: Building representations that support object classification performance and representations that preserve high-dimensional information about natural images are both important principles of the primate visual system.
claims.source: Prior work has indicated that building representations that support object classification performance and representations that preserve high-dimensional information about natural images are both important principles of the primate visual system (Cadieu et al., 2014; Elmoznino and Bonner, 2022; though see Conwell et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Cadieu et al., 2014; Elmoznino and Bonner, 2022; Conwell et al., 2022).

claims.claim: Artificial deep neural networks (DNNs) are the most predictive models of neural responses to images in the primate high-level visual cortex.
claims.source: Artificial deep neural networks (DNNs) are the most predictive models of neural responses to images in the primate high-level visual cortex (Cadieu et al., 2014; Schrimpf et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Cadieu et al., 2014; Schrimpf et al., 2020).

results.result: In the monkey ventral visual hierarchy, factorization of object identity from non-identity information (pose and background) increased from V4 to IT, and this factorization strongly contributed to object identity decoding performance. A lesion experiment demonstrated that reducing factorization while preserving invariance significantly impaired decoding accuracy.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C16-C20, C35, C49-C50 collectively provide strong converging evidence from neural recordings, statistical controls (shuffle), and a targeted lesion experiment. The lesion specifically manipulated factorization while controlling for other statistics, demonstrating its causal importance for decoding. The results are internally consistent and supported by appropriate controls.

results.result: Training DNNs consistently increased factorization of all tested scene parameters (background, lighting, object pose, camera viewpoint) relative to untrained networks. The degree of factorization in models correlated with their ability to predict IT neural activity, suggesting IT representations exhibit factorization. Training had mixed effects on invariance, increasing it for appearance factors but decreasing it for spatial transforms.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C25 are supported by systematic analysis across diverse DNN models with appropriate untrained controls (C21-C22). The correlation between model factorization and neural predictivity (C23) provides indirect but consistent evidence for factorization in IT (C24-C25). The inference about IT representations (C24-C25) is appropriately qualified as correlative evidence.

results.result: Across 12 datasets spanning monkey and human neural recordings, fMRI, and behavior, DNN models with greater factorization of scene parameters consistently matched biological data better. Invariance to appearance factors (background, lighting) correlated with brain-like models, but invariance to spatial transforms (pose, viewpoint) did not. These findings were robust to architecture, analysis method (encoding vs. RDM), factorization metric, and stimulus type (synthetic vs. natural movies).
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C26-C28, C36-C38, C51-C53 demonstrate remarkable consistency across multiple datasets, species, brain regions, and methodological variations. The extensive controls (architecture-matched models C51, RDM analysis C52, alternative factorization metric C53, natural movies C36-C37) and the differential pattern for invariance (C27-C28) strengthen confidence in the specificity of the factorization effect.

results.result: Factorization scores significantly improved prediction of neural and behavioral data beyond what could be explained by object classification performance or dimensionality alone. Combining factorization with classification performance provides better understanding of brain-like model properties than classification alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C31, C38 are supported by cross-validated regression analyses (Figure 6) that explicitly control for classification performance and dimensionality. The statistical approach appropriately tests whether factorization provides independent predictive power, and the results show it does across multiple datasets and analysis methods.

results.result: Simulation demonstrated that factorized representations (orthogonal encoding of variables) enable better generalization in few-shot decoding scenarios compared to non-factorized representations. High-dimensional representations facilitate factorization, and factorized representations better support classification.
results.evaluation: Claims C34, C39-C40 are supported by simulation data (Figure 1C) showing the computational benefits of factorization. The simulation appropriately isolates the effect of factorization (angle between variable subspaces) while controlling for other factors. The claims about relationships between dimensionality, factorization, and classification are logically consistent with the geometric framework.

results.result: The positive correlation between factorization and neural predictivity was robust to the choice of PCA threshold (50-99%) used to define the subspaces for computing factorization.
results.evaluation: Claim C29 is supported by sensitivity analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 3) showing consistent results across a wide range of threshold values. This addresses a potential methodological concern about arbitrary parameter choices in the PCA-based factorization metric.

results.result: Object classification has been proposed as a principal objective of the ventral visual stream and used as an optimization target for DNNs. DNNs trained for classification produce representations similar to primate V4 and IT, with similarity correlating with classification performance, though this relationship saturates beyond a threshold.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C11-C13, C57 accurately summarize established prior work with appropriate citations (Yamins et al., 2014; Schrimpf et al., 2020; Cadieu et al., 2014). These claims provide necessary context for the current work and are well-supported by the cited literature.

results.result: Visual brain areas represent many types of information beyond object identity, and optimizing for classification alone does not constrain how other information is encoded. High-level ventral stream neurons simultaneously encode multiple forms of information including object pose.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C14 are supported by established neuroscience knowledge and appropriate citations to prior work (Freiwald and Tsao, 2010; Hong et al., 2016; Kravitz et al., 2013; Peters and Kriegeskorte, 2021). These claims accurately represent the motivation for studying factorization as an alternative to pure invariance.

results.result: The authors' definition of factorization is closely related to manifold disentanglement and can be seen as a generalization to high-dimensional visual scene parameters like object pose.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C33 appropriately relate the current work to prior concepts (DiCarlo and Cox, 2007; Chung et al., 2018). The conceptual connection is reasonable and helps position the work within existing frameworks, though the generalization claim (C33) is somewhat inferential.

results.result: Factorization enables simultaneous decoding of multiple parameters supporting diverse behaviors, relates to the concept of abstraction in representational geometry, and is one factor determining few-shot classification performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C15, C42-C43 connect factorization to related concepts with appropriate citations (Johnston and Fusi, 2023; Bernardi et al., 2020; Sorscher et al., 2022). The connections are logical and help contextualize the functional significance of factorization, though some aspects are inferential (C42).

results.result: Local straightening of natural movies is important for early visual cortex but not necessarily high-level visual cortex, where factorization may play a role instead.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C45 appropriately cite prior work (Toosi and Issa, 2022) and make a reasonable inference about the complementary role of factorization in high-level cortex. The inference (C45) is appropriately qualified and consistent with the current findings.

results.result: Factorization increases with higher dimensionality because this decreases overlap between variable subspaces. In high dimensions, angles between points approach 90 degrees (orthogonality). For fixed dimensions, factorization is driven by the angle between variable subspaces.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 present mathematically sound reasoning about high-dimensional geometry. The claims about asymptotic behavior in high dimensions (C47) and the geometric basis of factorization (C48) are consistent with established mathematical principles and the authors' formal definitions.

results.result: Factorization of non-class information is an important strategy used by high-level visual cortex and by DNNs that predict primate neural and behavioral data.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 represent the main synthesis of findings from both neural data (Figure 2) and DNN analyses (Figures 4-5). These summary claims are well-supported by the convergent evidence from multiple experiments and datasets presented throughout the manuscript.

results.result: Prior work indicates that both supporting object classification performance and preserving high-dimensional information about natural images are important principles of the primate visual system.
results.evaluation: Claim C56 accurately summarizes prior work with appropriate citations (Cadieu et al., 2014; Elmoznino and Bonner, 2022; Conwell et al., 2022). The claim appropriately acknowledges some controversy ("though see Conwell et al., 2022") and provides context for the current contribution.

results.result: Machine learning models designed to infer disentangled representations displayed single-unit responses resembling individual macaque IT neurons.
results.evaluation: Claim C41 accurately cites prior work (Higgins et al., 2021) connecting disentanglement to neural responses. This provides relevant context for the relationship between factorization/disentanglement and biological neural representations.

results.result: Maintaining non-class information in factorized subspaces is often preferred to dropping it altogether, and factorization is a widely used strategy in brains and DNN models.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10 represent key interpretive conclusions supported by the differential effects of factorization versus invariance across datasets (C8, C27-C28). The inference that maintaining information in factorized form is "preferred" is reasonable given the consistent positive correlation of factorization but mixed results for invariance.

results.result: Factorization of object identity from non-identity information (pose, background) increases from V4 to IT in macaque visual cortex and is critical for object identity decoding performance. A lesion experiment showed that reducing factorization while preserving other statistics (invariance, covariance) strongly impaired decoding performance.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers accepted these findings without challenge. The editor states the analyses provide 'convincing evidence' for factorization in neural data. Reviewer 1 notes the paper 'uses a wide variety of datasets' with 'consistent' results showing 'great sign of robustness.' Reviewer 2 acknowledges the authors addressed prior weaknesses and thanks them for doing so.

results.result: Across 12 datasets spanning monkey and human neural/behavioral data, DNN models with higher factorization scores better predicted neural responses and behavior. Factorization explained variance in neural predictivity beyond what classification accuracy alone could account for (Figure 6), improving understanding of brainlike models.
results.evaluation: The editor describes this as a 'valuable empirical contribution' with 'convincing evidence that high factorization scores are correlated with neural predictivity.' Reviewer 1 emphasizes Figure 6 as 'the most important' and states factorization 'explains some variance in neural similarity that classification accuracy does not explain.' Reviewer 2 praises the 'systematic' analysis across datasets.

results.result: Invariance to scene parameters showed mixed correlations with neural predictivity: positive for appearance factors (background, lighting) but zero or negative for spatial transforms (pose, viewpoint). This suggests the brain maintains rather than discards non-class information in factorized subspaces.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these differential findings about invariance. The editor's statement that the work provides 'convincing evidence' encompasses both factorization and invariance results. Reviewer 1 notes the results are 'consistent across the datasets,' implicitly including the invariance patterns.

results.result: Training DNNs consistently increased factorization of all scene parameters relative to untrained networks, but produced mixed effects on invariance (increasing it for background/lighting, decreasing it for pose/viewpoint).
results.evaluation: These findings are presented as part of the systematic DNN analysis that reviewers praised. Reviewer 2 specifically commends 'the authors' efforts in systematically conducting analysis' and notes the 'definition of factorization is simple and intuitive to understand,' supporting acceptance of how training affects these metrics.

results.result: The main findings were robust to methodological choices: different PCA thresholds for quantifying factorization, using only ResNet-50 architecture, using RDMs instead of linear regression fits, and using covariance-based versus PCA-based factorization metrics.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly praises the authors' transparency and notes they 'are very transparent, particularly in the supplementary material, showing results on all datasets. This is excellent practice.' The robustness analyses are part of this transparent reporting that reviewers accepted without objection.

results.result: Factorization of frame-by-frame variance (local temporal changes, likely motion) from other variance sources in natural movies correlated with improved neural predictivity in both macaque and human data.
results.evaluation: This extension to natural movie stimuli is part of the broad dataset analysis that reviewers praised. Reviewer 1 states 'This paper uses a wide variety of datasets, spanning multiple brain areas and species. The results are consistent across the datasets,' which encompasses the natural movie findings.

results.result: The authors propose that factorization of visual scene information is a widely used strategy in both biological visual systems and predictive DNN models, representing an important organizational principle alongside invariance.
results.evaluation: The editor states this work 'will be of interest to systems neuroscientists studying vision and could inspire further research.' Reviewer 1 notes 'This paper challenges the dominant approach to modeling neural responses in the ventral stream, which itself is valuable for diversifying the space of ideas,' affirming the conceptual contribution.

results.result: Simulations demonstrated that factorized representations (orthogonal encoding) enable better generalization for decoding multiple variables from few training samples, and that high-dimensional representations facilitate factorization while factorized representations support classification.
results.evaluation: These conceptual/simulation results supporting the main empirical findings are not challenged by reviewers. Reviewer 2 notes 'the definition of factorization is simple and intuitive to understand,' suggesting acceptance of the conceptual framework including these supporting simulations.

results.result: Background claims establishing that object classification has been the dominant objective for modeling ventral stream, that DNNs trained on classification match neural data but plateau in predictivity, and that visual neurons encode multiple types of information beyond object identity.
results.evaluation: These are established background claims from prior literature that frame the motivation. Reviewer 1 explicitly acknowledges this context, stating 'beyond a certain threshold level of object classification performance, further improvement fails to produce a concomitant improvement in predicting primate neural responses... This suggests that classification performance may not be a sufficient objective.'

results.result: Conceptual claims relating factorization to prior concepts (disentanglement, abstraction, manifold geometry) and discussing functional benefits (supporting diverse behaviors, few-shot learning) and mathematical properties of factorization in high-dimensional spaces.
results.evaluation: These conceptual connections and theoretical discussions are not challenged by reviewers. Reviewer 2 notes the work explores factorization 'which has strong connections with emerging concepts like disentanglement and abstraction,' affirming these conceptual links are appropriate.
